bull_bear.body:
- Integrated/downstream structure: alcohol and cogeneration plants using molasses and bagasse 'continue to complement the profitability of the company' and de-risk sugar cyclicality
- Added flexibility to produce ethanol from sugarcane juice/syrup, not only molasses
- Robust sugarcane extension department supporting field crop management, plus an R&D wing that develops and supplies new high-yielding, disease-free varieties to farmers
- Cane development programme: above 90% of the area maintained with high yield and high sugar varieties; village-level yield support raised average yield by 1.80 to 4.0 tonnes per acre in 46 villages in FY 2025-26
- Mechanical harvesting covering 15% of total cane harvesting, with entrepreneur development and further harvester development in progress
- Recovery improved to 8.73% in FY 2025-26 from 8.14%, against a Tamil Nadu state average that fell from 8.75% to 8.15%
- 100% retention of key management talent in the year, with staff attrition at 12.19% versus 13.93% in the previous year
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Sugarcane availability — climate-dependent and structurally shrinking in Tamil Nadu — Sugarcane is the main raw material and is monsoon dependent. Climate variation cut Tamil Nadu cane availability from 123 lakh tons to 84 lakh tons and the company's own crushing fell to 11.29 lakh tons from 12.29 lakh tons. The MD&A notes intense summer in H1 2024 and Cyclone Fengal in November 2024 depressed planting, with a 12-month gestation lag that carried the shortfall into January-March 2026. Scarcity of harvest labour and the availability of attractive competing crops with remunerative prices compound the risk.
- Sugar recovery below the FRP peg — a structural loss per ton of cane in Tamil Nadu — The Board perceives the risk of recurring lower sugar recovery in Tamil Nadu compared with the minimum recovery at which mills must pay the Fair and Remunerative Price. TN mills must pay FRP at 9.50% irrespective of actual recovery — paying for 95 kg of sugar equivalent while recovering only 81.5 kg. The gap between FRP payable and RSF value is Rs 321 per ton of cane which mills are unable to recover, and 'the loss works out to Rs 535 per ton of cane crushed'.
- Low capacity utilisation and fixed-cost absorption — 'The capacity utilization is around 33% which has resulted in the sub-optimal production of sugar, power and alcohol. Accordingly, the incidence of fixed cost has more than tripled compared to normal times, leaving correspondingly lower amount in the hands of mills for cane payment.' The Board separately records that lower capacity utilisation is a concern.
- Financial liquidity — operating without consortium working capital while under lender monitoring — The Company has been under a monitoring period since the debt restructuring implemented by lenders with retrospective effect from 30.06.2020, is operating without working capital facilities from the consortium lenders, and has to continuously sell inventory to maintain cash flows; this will continue until its account is upgraded as standard. The sugar industry is highly working capital intensive and management flags that raising adequate and rightly-priced working capital for peak-period operation might pose a challenge. Mitigation is the restructuring's beneficial terms (reduced interest rate, deferred repayment) plus a Rs 30 crore Dropline Overdraft repayable over 21 months and a Rs 20 crore Cash Credit from Kotak Mahindra Bank.
- Government regulation of sugar pricing and release — including litigation the company has lost at first instance — The industry is regulated on cane area reservation, cane price fixation, the monthly sugar release mechanism, an MSP of Rs 31/kg, and export quotas. The Company challenged the monthly sugar release mechanism in court; the Madras High Court dismissed its writ petition and the Company filed a writ appeal on 24.10.2024, which is pending disposal. The Board notes Government policy on sugar will continue to have a significant bearing on the prospects of the industry.
- Distillery / ENA revenue displaced by inter-state imports into Tamil Nadu — The Tamil Nadu government has been allowing IMFL manufacturers to import a major share of their Extra Neutral Alcohol requirement from neighbouring states at comparatively lower tax rates, giving other states an unfair advantage and adversely affecting the cash flow stream of TN sugar manufacturers, since ENA is one of the main revenue streams. Tamil Nadu's option to shift into ethanol is also limited by restricted molasses availability.
- Sugar price realisation and cyclicality — Price realisation is one of the industry's major risks, though management judges the perceived risk 'lower given the outlook of lower stock available'. Mitigation is structural — downstream alcohol and cogeneration using molasses and bagasse to complement profitability, added flexibility to make ethanol from cane juice/syrup, and selling sugar regularly at every price point to improve average realisation.
- Climate and weather volatility ahead — 'The unpredictable climate variations, rainfall pattern & low recovery are threats to the sustainable operation of the Industry. International weather pattern suggests that this year would be a worst El Nino Year in the last 140 years.' The company mitigates with drip irrigation, water gel application, trash shredding/mulching, focus on areas with better ground water availability and drought-tolerant varietal work.

outlook.body:
- De-risk sugar cyclicality through the downstream plants — alcohol and cogeneration of power using molasses and bagasse — which management says continue to complement the profitability of the company
- Retain flexibility to produce ethanol from sugarcane juice/syrup, in addition to molasses, now that the Central Government has lifted the ban on ethanol from cane juice and B heavy molasses
- Sell sugar regularly at every price point to improve average realization rather than timing the market
- Secure cane supply through a cane development programme: subsidy to farmers for planting, service providers for cultivation operations, timely supply of quality seed material, and a gradual increase in registered cane with reduction of outside cane
- Push mechanisation — mechanical harvesting (15% of total cane harvesting, with entrepreneur development), wider row planting (42% to 69% coverage across all three units in new planting areas) and mechanised inter-cultural operations
- Improve recovery and yield through R&D: Sweet Bloom 2.0 with ICAR-Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Adaptive Research Trials with TNAU, AICRP clone evaluation at Varadaraj Nagar and Mundiyampakkam, and sourcing East Coast Zone clones from SRS Vyyuru for clay soils
- Adopt precision-agriculture technology — automated drip fertigation with weather stations, soil moisture sensors and field cameras on an 11-acre R&D block, and soil nutrient based fertility mapping in the Mundiyampakkam command area
- Promote drip irrigation, trash shredding, trash mulching and organic manure application to protect yield against erratic rainfall and drought
- Digital and outreach-based technology transfer to farmers — an exclusive Rajshree Sugars YouTube channel and the restart of Audio Visual Van programmes after a six-year gap
- Restore financial flexibility: continue the approved debt restructuring with lenders and work towards upgradation of loan accounts to standard, having availed interim working capital from Kotak Mahindra Bank
- Focus on factory efficiency parameters to recover maximum sugar, and concentrate cane development in areas with better ground water availability
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The annual report discloses no new plant, capacity-addition or greenfield/brownfield expansion project. The Company operates its existing three units — Unit I, Unit II (Mundiyampakkam) and Unit III — with cogeneration at Unit II and Unit III and a power plant at Gingee that exports to the State Grid under a PPA, and states that capacity is under-utilised (Tamil Nadu industry capacity utilisation around 33%) rather than being expanded. The only footprint additions described are agricultural and R&D in nature: 15.38 acres taken on lease at Koliyanur division, Mundiyampakkam to augment varietal research and production of quality high-sugar variety seed, and an automated drip fertigation system with an automatic weather station, soil moisture sensors and field cameras installed on an 11-acre block of the R&D Farm on a trial basis, which the company says it is studying 'for further expansion'. Drip irrigation coverage was extended across 1,080 acres at Unit I, 547 acres at Unit II and 356 acres at Unit III. The Company added flexibility to produce ethanol from sugarcane juice/syrup after the Central Government lifted the ban on ethanol from cane juice and B heavy molasses, but no ethanol capacity project, cost or commissioning date is disclosed. On the balance-sheet side the note on capital and other commitments records no estimated amount of contracts remaining to be executed on capital account and not provided for, and all loans/facilities from Axis Bank were repaid during the year, subject to Right of Recompense per the Axis Bank sanction letter dated 30-06-2021.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Domestic sugar price: 'The increase in domestic prices due to lower production and firm World sugar prices, continues to be an opportunity for the industry to sustain and increase margins'; with production in Maharashtra and north Karnataka lower than estimated, domestic prices took an upswing in the current season
- Perceived risk on sugar price realization is lower given the outlook of lower stock available
- Cane availability is the binding constraint — Tamil Nadu cane availability fell from 123 lakh tons to 84 lakh tons and state recovery from 8.75% to 8.15%; the company crushed 11.29 lakh tons versus 12.29 lakh tons, though its own recovery improved to 8.73% from 8.14%
- Ground water recharge in the Company's command areas has been encouraging for cane planting, supporting factory operations for at least the next two years
- Structural TN margin squeeze: capacity utilisation around 33% has tripled the incidence of fixed cost, and mills must pay FRP pegged to 9.50% recovery — paying for 95 kg of sugar equivalent while recovering only 81.5 kg — a loss of Rs 535 per ton of cane crushed
- Ethanol blending programme remains supportive: OMCs blended 1040 crore litres in EY 2024-25 (19.24% national average) and 328 crore litres to 31 March 2026 (19.98%); draft flexi-fuel rules of April 2026 propose higher blends including E85 and E100, though this requires automotive manufacturers to introduce appropriate engine technology
- Cogeneration realisation improves on the TNERC tariff order of 22.09.2025 raising the Gingee rate to Rs 6.59 per unit from Rs 5.72; Mundiyampakkam power is sold to third-party customers, ensuring timely payment and supporting working capital
- Distillery/ENA demand is being displaced — Tamil Nadu allows IMFL manufacturers to import a major share of ENA from neighbouring states at lower tax rates, hurting TN mills' cash flow, and higher alcohol stocking resulted
- Government policy remains decisive — monthly sugar release mechanism, MSP of Rs 31/kg, and approved exports of 1.5 million tons for the 2025-26 season; 'the Government policy on sugar would continue to have a significant bearing on the prospects of the industry in the coming years'
- Threats: unpredictable climate variations, rainfall pattern and low recovery; international weather pattern suggests this year would be the worst El Nino year in the last 140 years
- Emergence of competitive crops with remunerative prices could pose a threat to sugarcane cultivation
- Sugar industry is highly working capital intensive; raising adequate and rightly-priced working capital to support peak-period operation might pose a challenge

open.item: The Company remains under the monitoring period following the debt restructuring implemented by lenders with retrospective effect from 30.06.2020 and will continue to operate without consortium working capital facilities, selling inventory continuously to maintain cash flows, until its account is upgraded as standard with the lenders.

The Company has availed a Dropline Overdraft and Cash Credit from Kotak Mahindra Bank secured by a first pari passu charge on all fixed assets of Unit-III and on all current assets except Unit-II and Unit-III cogeneration receivables, with the Cash Credit to be taken over by consortium lenders upon upgradation of loan accounts.
Management flags that the emergence of competitive crops with remunerative prices could pose a threat to sugarcane cultivation in its command areas.

Management flags unpredictable climate variations, rainfall pattern and low recovery as threats to sustainable operation, noting international weather patterns suggest this year would be the worst El Nino year in the last 140 years.

A pilot soil nutrient based fertility mapping programme has been initiated in the Unit-2 Mundiyampakkam command area, with 2,200 samples collected covering all sugarcane growing villages and analysis under progress, to help farmers with low fertile lands improve soil conditions.

The company is exploring AI-driven automation — drip fertigation integrated with automatic weather stations and soil moisture sensors, installed on an 11-acre block of the R&D farm on a trial basis — to study efficacy on cane yield and quality and for further expansion.

The company is running multi-stage varietal research to identify high-yield, high-sugar varieties for its command areas — Sweet Bloom 2.0 with ICAR-SBI, adaptive trials with TNAU, and evaluation of AICRP clone sets — with a new set of 16 clones (AICRP 22000 series) taken up for initial multiplication in March 2026 at Varadaraj Nagar for further evaluation.
The company will continue to rely on its downstream alcohol and cogeneration plants — and on newly added flexibility to produce ethanol from sugarcane juice/syrup — to de-risk sugar cyclicality.
The Company's writ appeal filed before the Madras High Court on 24.10.2024 against the monthly sugar release mechanism, seeking to set aside the single judge's order, is pending disposal.
The Company is focusing on selling sugar regularly at every price point thereby improving average realization.

The company is taking special measures to protect cane supply — providing subsidy to farmers for cane planting, appointing service providers for cultivation operations, promoting mechanical harvesting, wider row planting, drip irrigation, trash shredding/mulching and organic manure application, and arranging timely supply of quality seed material.

The Board flags that the Tamil Nadu government allowing IMFL manufacturers to import a major share of their ENA requirement from neighbouring states gives other states an unfair advantage and adversely affects the cash flow stream of Tamil Nadu sugar manufacturers.

Management flags that Tamil Nadu mills must pay FRP pegged to a minimum 9.50% recovery irrespective of actual recovery, leaving a gap of Rs 321 per ton of cane between FRP payable and RSF value which mills are unable to recover, with the loss working out to Rs 535 per ton of cane crushed.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Sugar:** Sugar
- **Cogeneration:** Power exported to third-party customers, Power exported to the State Grid under a power purchase agreement
- **Distillery:** Alcohol, Ethanol (including from sugarcane juice/syrup), Extra Neutral Alcohol (ENA)

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- Domestic Indian sugar market (monthly sugar release mechanism, MSP of Rs 31/kg)
- Oil Marketing Companies via the Central Government ethanol blending programme
- Indian Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) manufacturers in Tamil Nadu, who buy ENA
- Third-party power customers and the Tamil Nadu State Grid
- India only — revenue from sales to customers outside India is nil

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Domestic sugar price: 'The increase in domestic prices due to lower production and firm World sugar prices, continues to be an opportunity for the industry to sustain and increase margins'; with production in Maharashtra and north Karnataka lower than estimated, domestic prices took an upswing in the current season
- Perceived risk on sugar price realization is lower given the outlook of lower stock available
- Cane availability is the binding constraint — Tamil Nadu cane availability fell from 123 lakh tons to 84 lakh tons and state recovery from 8.75% to 8.15%; the company crushed 11.29 lakh tons versus 12.29 lakh tons, though its own recovery improved to 8.73% from 8.14%
- Ground water recharge in the Company's command areas has been encouraging for cane planting, supporting factory operations for at least the next two years
- Structural TN margin squeeze: capacity utilisation around 33% has tripled the incidence of fixed cost, and mills must pay FRP pegged to 9.50% recovery — paying for 95 kg of sugar equivalent while recovering only 81.5 kg — a loss of Rs 535 per ton of cane crushed
- Ethanol blending programme remains supportive: OMCs blended 1040 crore litres in EY 2024-25 (19.24% national average) and 328 crore litres to 31 March 2026 (19.98%); draft flexi-fuel rules of April 2026 propose higher blends including E85 and E100, though this requires automotive manufacturers to introduce appropriate engine technology
- Cogeneration realisation improves on the TNERC tariff order of 22.09.2025 raising the Gingee rate to Rs 6.59 per unit from Rs 5.72; Mundiyampakkam power is sold to third-party customers, ensuring timely payment and supporting working capital
- Distillery/ENA demand is being displaced — Tamil Nadu allows IMFL manufacturers to import a major share of ENA from neighbouring states at lower tax rates, hurting TN mills' cash flow, and higher alcohol stocking resulted
- Government policy remains decisive — monthly sugar release mechanism, MSP of Rs 31/kg, and approved exports of 1.5 million tons for the 2025-26 season; 'the Government policy on sugar would continue to have a significant bearing on the prospects of the industry in the coming years'
- Threats: unpredictable climate variations, rainfall pattern and low recovery; international weather pattern suggests this year would be the worst El Nino year in the last 140 years
- Emergence of competitive crops with remunerative prices could pose a threat to sugarcane cultivation
- Sugar industry is highly working capital intensive; raising adequate and rightly-priced working capital to support peak-period operation might pose a challenge

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- De-risk sugar cyclicality through the downstream plants — alcohol and cogeneration of power using molasses and bagasse — which management says continue to complement the profitability of the company
- Retain flexibility to produce ethanol from sugarcane juice/syrup, in addition to molasses, now that the Central Government has lifted the ban on ethanol from cane juice and B heavy molasses
- Sell sugar regularly at every price point to improve average realization rather than timing the market
- Secure cane supply through a cane development programme: subsidy to farmers for planting, service providers for cultivation operations, timely supply of quality seed material, and a gradual increase in registered cane with reduction of outside cane
- Push mechanisation — mechanical harvesting (15% of total cane harvesting, with entrepreneur development), wider row planting (42% to 69% coverage across all three units in new planting areas) and mechanised inter-cultural operations
- Improve recovery and yield through R&D: Sweet Bloom 2.0 with ICAR-Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Adaptive Research Trials with TNAU, AICRP clone evaluation at Varadaraj Nagar and Mundiyampakkam, and sourcing East Coast Zone clones from SRS Vyyuru for clay soils
- Adopt precision-agriculture technology — automated drip fertigation with weather stations, soil moisture sensors and field cameras on an 11-acre R&D block, and soil nutrient based fertility mapping in the Mundiyampakkam command area
- Promote drip irrigation, trash shredding, trash mulching and organic manure application to protect yield against erratic rainfall and drought
- Digital and outreach-based technology transfer to farmers — an exclusive Rajshree Sugars YouTube channel and the restart of Audio Visual Van programmes after a six-year gap
- Restore financial flexibility: continue the approved debt restructuring with lenders and work towards upgradation of loan accounts to standard, having availed interim working capital from Kotak Mahindra Bank
- Focus on factory efficiency parameters to recover maximum sugar, and concentrate cane development in areas with better ground water availability

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The annual report discloses no new plant, capacity-addition or greenfield/brownfield expansion project. The Company operates its existing three units — Unit I, Unit II (Mundiyampakkam) and Unit III — with cogeneration at Unit II and Unit III and a power plant at Gingee that exports to the State Grid under a PPA, and states that capacity is under-utilised (Tamil Nadu industry capacity utilisation around 33%) rather than being expanded. The only footprint additions described are agricultural and R&D in nature: 15.38 acres taken on lease at Koliyanur division, Mundiyampakkam to augment varietal research and production of quality high-sugar variety seed, and an automated drip fertigation system with an automatic weather station, soil moisture sensors and field cameras installed on an 11-acre block of the R&D Farm on a trial basis, which the company says it is studying 'for further expansion'. Drip irrigation coverage was extended across 1,080 acres at Unit I, 547 acres at Unit II and 356 acres at Unit III. The Company added flexibility to produce ethanol from sugarcane juice/syrup after the Central Government lifted the ban on ethanol from cane juice and B heavy molasses, but no ethanol capacity project, cost or commissioning date is disclosed. On the balance-sheet side the note on capital and other commitments records no estimated amount of contracts remaining to be executed on capital account and not provided for, and all loans/facilities from Axis Bank were repaid during the year, subject to Right of Recompense per the Axis Bank sanction letter dated 30-06-2021.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Integrated/downstream structure: alcohol and cogeneration plants using molasses and bagasse 'continue to complement the profitability of the company' and de-risk sugar cyclicality
- Added flexibility to produce ethanol from sugarcane juice/syrup, not only molasses
- Robust sugarcane extension department supporting field crop management, plus an R&D wing that develops and supplies new high-yielding, disease-free varieties to farmers
- Cane development programme: above 90% of the area maintained with high yield and high sugar varieties; village-level yield support raised average yield by 1.80 to 4.0 tonnes per acre in 46 villages in FY 2025-26
- Mechanical harvesting covering 15% of total cane harvesting, with entrepreneur development and further harvester development in progress
- Recovery improved to 8.73% in FY 2025-26 from 8.14%, against a Tamil Nadu state average that fell from 8.75% to 8.15%
- 100% retention of key management talent in the year, with staff attrition at 12.19% versus 13.93% in the previous year

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Sugarcane availability — climate-dependent and structurally shrinking in Tamil Nadu — Sugarcane is the main raw material and is monsoon dependent. Climate variation cut Tamil Nadu cane availability from 123 lakh tons to 84 lakh tons and the company's own crushing fell to 11.29 lakh tons from 12.29 lakh tons. The MD&A notes intense summer in H1 2024 and Cyclone Fengal in November 2024 depressed planting, with a 12-month gestation lag that carried the shortfall into January-March 2026. Scarcity of harvest labour and the availability of attractive competing crops with remunerative prices compound the risk.
- Sugar recovery below the FRP peg — a structural loss per ton of cane in Tamil Nadu — The Board perceives the risk of recurring lower sugar recovery in Tamil Nadu compared with the minimum recovery at which mills must pay the Fair and Remunerative Price. TN mills must pay FRP at 9.50% irrespective of actual recovery — paying for 95 kg of sugar equivalent while recovering only 81.5 kg. The gap between FRP payable and RSF value is Rs 321 per ton of cane which mills are unable to recover, and 'the loss works out to Rs 535 per ton of cane crushed'.
- Low capacity utilisation and fixed-cost absorption — 'The capacity utilization is around 33% which has resulted in the sub-optimal production of sugar, power and alcohol. Accordingly, the incidence of fixed cost has more than tripled compared to normal times, leaving correspondingly lower amount in the hands of mills for cane payment.' The Board separately records that lower capacity utilisation is a concern.
- Financial liquidity — operating without consortium working capital while under lender monitoring — The Company has been under a monitoring period since the debt restructuring implemented by lenders with retrospective effect from 30.06.2020, is operating without working capital facilities from the consortium lenders, and has to continuously sell inventory to maintain cash flows; this will continue until its account is upgraded as standard. The sugar industry is highly working capital intensive and management flags that raising adequate and rightly-priced working capital for peak-period operation might pose a challenge. Mitigation is the restructuring's beneficial terms (reduced interest rate, deferred repayment) plus a Rs 30 crore Dropline Overdraft repayable over 21 months and a Rs 20 crore Cash Credit from Kotak Mahindra Bank.
- Government regulation of sugar pricing and release — including litigation the company has lost at first instance — The industry is regulated on cane area reservation, cane price fixation, the monthly sugar release mechanism, an MSP of Rs 31/kg, and export quotas. The Company challenged the monthly sugar release mechanism in court; the Madras High Court dismissed its writ petition and the Company filed a writ appeal on 24.10.2024, which is pending disposal. The Board notes Government policy on sugar will continue to have a significant bearing on the prospects of the industry.
- Distillery / ENA revenue displaced by inter-state imports into Tamil Nadu — The Tamil Nadu government has been allowing IMFL manufacturers to import a major share of their Extra Neutral Alcohol requirement from neighbouring states at comparatively lower tax rates, giving other states an unfair advantage and adversely affecting the cash flow stream of TN sugar manufacturers, since ENA is one of the main revenue streams. Tamil Nadu's option to shift into ethanol is also limited by restricted molasses availability.
- Sugar price realisation and cyclicality — Price realisation is one of the industry's major risks, though management judges the perceived risk 'lower given the outlook of lower stock available'. Mitigation is structural — downstream alcohol and cogeneration using molasses and bagasse to complement profitability, added flexibility to make ethanol from cane juice/syrup, and selling sugar regularly at every price point to improve average realisation.
- Climate and weather volatility ahead — 'The unpredictable climate variations, rainfall pattern & low recovery are threats to the sustainable operation of the Industry. International weather pattern suggests that this year would be a worst El Nino Year in the last 140 years.' The company mitigates with drip irrigation, water gel application, trash shredding/mulching, focus on areas with better ground water availability and drought-tolerant varietal work.

hero.oneLiner: Rajshree Sugars & Chemicals is a Tamil Nadu-based integrated sugar producer operating three segments — Sugar, Cogeneration and Distillery — which crushed 11.29 lakh tons of cane in FY 2025-26.
